en: The Scripture on the Explanation of the Sections Spoken by the Buddha, in one fascicle;
translated by Paramārtha, the Tripiṭaka Master from Central India during the Chen Dynasty.
Chapter One: The Ineffable Non-duality. The First Chapter: The Ineffable Non-duality.
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha Bhagavān was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of ninety-nine thousand bhikṣus. All were arhats—whose outflows were exhausted, who had accomplished what was to be done, laid down their heavy burdens, attained their own benefit, destroyed the fetters of existence, whose minds were well-liberated, who had attained mastery, and who were well-versed in śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Their names were: the venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya and others, up to Subhūti and others who dwelt in the āraṇa-samādhi.
Furthermore, there was an assembly of thirty-six thousand great bhikṣuṇīs together, headed by Mahāprajāpatī and including Bhikṣuṇī Bhadrakāpilānī and others.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable and innumerable *upāsakas* and *upāsikās*, with King Bimbisāra as their leader.

There were also immeasurable hundreds of thousands of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the assembly of bodhisattvas within this Bhadrakalpa, some residing in this land and others coming from other directions, with Maitreya Bodhisattva, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, and others as their leaders—all of whom had thoroughly penetrated the profoundly deep nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), were disciplined and easy to transform, practiced equanimity well, cultivated the bodhisattva path, served as true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) to all sentient beings, had attained unimpeded *dhāraṇīs*, turned the irreversible wheel of Dharma, and had already made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas.
When this assembly had thus gathered together,
the Bodhisattva Yathārtha-śravaṇa addressed the Bodhisattva Gambhīrārtha-vibhakti-jña, saying:
"O Son of the Buddha!..."
"All dharmas are non-dual.
Regarding the statement that 'all dharmas are non-dual,' what does this mean?
The Bodhisattva Gambhīrārthapadapravicaya replied:
“Good son! All these dharmas do not exceed these two: namely, that which is created and that which is uncreated.
That which is created is neither uncreated nor non-uncreated.”
"It is not that which is created, nor is it that which is not created, nor is it both created and not created.
Thus addressed, the Bodhisattva Yathārthaśravaṇa asked:
"O Son of the Buddha!"
"What is that which is both what is done and not what is done, yet not not-what-is-done;
and that which is neither not-what-is-done nor not-not-what-is-done, and yet is also not what is done?
The Bodhisattva Gambhīrārthapadavibhaṅga replied:

“Good son! That which is ‘created’ refers to the words and phrases of the Great Teacher’s authentic teaching. If they are words and phrases of the Great Teacher’s authentic teaching, they are nevertheless worldly designations that arise from conceptual discrimination.”

If the verbal expressions of this world arise from conceptual construction, they are entirely unestablished due to various constructions and the expressions themselves; therefore, they are not something produced.
"O son of good family!

That which is not something to be produced is subsumed under verbal instruction; if there is a dharma that transcends both what is to be produced and what is not to be produced, that dharma is likewise, and likewise.
"If it is so, would the Great Teacher’s teaching not be without meaning?
"It is not without meaning.
"If it has meaning, what is the nature of that meaning?"

That which is called the ineffable essence is realized only by the non-conceptual knowledge and vision of the Sage; yet, for the purpose of enabling others to thoroughly understand this ineffable essence, [the Sage employs conventional designations].
Therefore, the Great Teacher spoke these words of instruction, saying: "This is what is produced by phenomena.
Son of good family!

That which is not produced is the true teaching and expression of the Great Teacher; yet if it were the true teaching and expression of the Great Teacher, it would be a conventional designation established in the world, arising from conceptual discrimination."

If the conventional expressions of this world arise from conceptualization, they would be entirely unestablished due to various forms of conceptualization and the speech resulting therefrom; therefore, they are not non-produced.
"O son of good family!..."
That which is "produced" is subsumed under verbal teaching; if there were any phenomenon apart from the unproduced and the produced, that phenomenon would likewise be thus and thus.
"If that is so, would the Great Teacher’s teaching not be without meaning?
"It is not without meaning.
"If it has meaning, what are the characteristics of that meaning?"

That which is called the ineffable essence is realized only by the non-conceptual knowledge and vision of the Sage; yet, desiring to cause others to thoroughly understand this ineffable essence, [he employs conventional designations].
Therefore, the Great Teacher spoke these instructions, saying: "This Dharma is not something created. "Good son!

It is like a skilled illusionist or his apprentice who, at a crossroads, takes grass, leaves, wood, stones, and so forth, gathers them together in one place, and manifests various illusory phenomena:"
The various elephant troops, cavalry, chariot troops, and infantry; the mani-jewels, pearls, coral, jade, and stones; as well as the granaries, treasuries, and so forth.

If there are certain people—infants, ordinary worldlings, or those of foolish and perverted wisdom—who cannot discern that grass and such things are the basis of the illusion, then when they see or hear [of them], they will think:
"Truly, these elephants, horses, the fourfold army, and the treasuries exist."
Whether seeing or hearing, they adhere to what they have seen or heard according to their ability and strength, making such declarations:
"This is the truth; anything other than this is not true."
That person should then reconsider this further.

If there are people who are not infants, ordinary worldlings, or those of foolish and perverted wisdom—who recognize that such grasses and other things are the basis of the illusion—and who, upon seeing or hearing them, reflect thus:
"There are no such things as these elephants, horses, and so forth, nor are there any treasuries."
If such a person sees or hears [these things], they act according to their ability and strength, yet remain unattached to what is seen or heard, speaking thus:
"According to my contemplation, this is the truth; anything other than this is not true."
"Although this follows worldly speech, it is for the purpose of revealing the ultimate meaning; such a person need not contemplate it further. Good son!
Just as these infants and ordinary worldlings have not yet attained the supramundane noble wisdom of *tathatā* (suchness), they do not recognize that the essence of all phenomena is ineffable."
If such a person sees or hears of the various phenomena that are produced and those that are not produced, they reflect thus:
"Truly, there exist such phenomena that are produced and those that are not produced."
Why is this? Because it can be seen and known.
If such a person sees or hears something, they become attached to what they have seen or heard according to their capacity and strength, and speak in accordance with what they have seen or heard:
"This is the truth; anything other than this is not true.
Such a person ought to reflect upon this deeply.

"If there are those who are neither infants nor ordinary worldlings—who have already seen the truth, attained the supramundane noble wisdom of suchness, and recognized that the essence of all phenomena is ineffable—and yet, whether seeing or hearing [these teachings], they entertain such thoughts:"

"As it is seen and known, all phenomena—whether conditioned or unconditioned—are not truly existent; they possess only conventional designations, arising from conceptual discrimination like magical illusions that deceive the minds of ordinary people. Within these, one gives rise to the names 'conditioned' and 'unconditioned,' as well as other various names."
This person, according to what they have seen and heard, does not give rise to attachment, nor do they say:
"This is the truth; anything other than this is not true.
Although they conform to worldly speech for the sake of clarifying the true meaning, this person has no need to deliberate upon it further.

“Good son! Thus, by means of noble knowledge and vision, these noble ones have already awakened to the ineffable essence. Desiring to cause others to see the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), they therefore speak words of instruction, such as ‘that which is created’ and ‘that which is uncreated,’ and so forth.”
At that time, the Bodhisattva Able to Resolve Profound Doctrinal Points spoke these verses:
“The Dharma spoken by the Buddha transcends words; It is non-dual and not within the sphere of ordinary beings.”
Fools are deluded therein; clinging to duality and engaging in conceptual proliferation, they fail to resolve what is false and thus perpetually wander through the realms of existence.
The wise person, free from [reliance on] seeing and hearing, discerns the true meaning within.
Chapter 2: Transcending the Sphere of Vitarka and Vicāra. At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

From this Sahā world, proceeding toward the east to the most distant world in the eastern direction, beyond seventy-seven worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there is a world called Suvikhyāta, where the Buddha named Mahāvikhyāta Sugata resides.

At one time, I went to that Buddha’s abode, where I saw in one part of the ground seventy-seven thousand followers of external paths gathered and seated with their teacher at their head, desiring to deliberate upon the true nature of all phenomena.

At that time, the assembly of non-Buddhists contemplated and deliberated, discerning and establishing the true nature of all phenomena; yet, relying on their own teachings, they sought the true nature but none were able to find it.

They gave rise to various attachments, engaging in conflicting disputes and even verbal hostility; by means of the swords and staves of their speech, they wounded and destroyed one another, and then each dispersed.
Having seen this, I reflected: "How marvelous! How marvelous!

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have appeared in the world; because of the appearance of the Buddhas, the profound characteristics of phenomena—which transcend the sphere of vitarka and vicāra—have been fully realized and clearly manifested."
After the Bodhisattva had finished speaking, the Buddha immediately said to him:
“So it is, Dharmodgata! Suchness (tathatā) is beyond the sphere of vitarka and vicāra.”
Having realized this myself, I explain it for others, establishing the true teaching, revealing and manifesting it so that its meaning becomes shallow and easy to understand.
Why is this? What I speak of as reality is that which is personally realized and seen only by the noble ones.
If it were within the sphere of discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*) of ordinary beings, it could be realized by both oneself and others.
Dharmodgata! For this reason, you should know that the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) transcends all spheres of discursive thought.
"Furthermore, Dharmodgata! I say that the sphere of activity of reality is without marks;
it is the sphere of activity of all discursive thoughts and conditions of marks."
For this reason, you should know that the true mark transcends the sphere of vitarka and vicāra.
"Furthermore, Dharmodgata! I say that reality is ineffable."
"All conceptualizations and discursive thoughts arise solely from verbal expression;
therefore, know that the true mark transcends the sphere of conceptualization and discursive thought. Furthermore, Dharmodgata!"
I say that true reality is beyond the four matters, namely: what is seen, heard, sensed, and known;
all discursive thought arises conditioned by these four matters.
"Furthermore, Dharmodgata!..."
I teach that the true reality is free from all strife;
for all discursive thought and investigation are the realms of strife.
For this reason, one should know that the true reality transcends the sphere of discursive thought and investigation.

“Dharmodgata! For example, suppose there were a person who, throughout their entire lifespan, constantly ate bitter flavors; it would be impossible for them to then perceive, contemplate, infer, or remember the sweet taste of honey and the like.”

"Furthermore, it is like a person who constantly delights in sensory desires and is scorched by the burning heat of those desires; for such a person to be able to engage in applied and sustained thought, to deliberate, and to maintain mindfulness without taking sensory signs as objects, relying instead on internal seclusion and bliss—this is impossible."

"Furthermore, it is like a person who constantly delights in verbal disputes and engages in perverse talk and jesting; for such a person to be able to practice discernment and reflection, to engage in inference, and to maintain the noble silence of meditative concentration—this is impossible."

"Furthermore, for example, suppose there were a person who constantly delights in and constantly practices seeing, hearing, perceiving, and cognizing; yet, while being able to engage in applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), inference, and mindfulness, they claim to transcend the four bases of consciousness, extinguish and depart from the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), and thereby attain *parinirvāṇa*—this is impossible.
"Furthermore, Dharmodgata!

It is as if there were a person who, because he constantly accumulates wealth and delights in waging war, yet is able to apply directed thought and sustained contemplation, to engage in inference, and to maintain mindfulness of Uttarakuru—a place where there is no sense of 'mine,' no accumulation of possessions, and no mutual strife—as being a bliss of the present life; such a thing is impossible."

“Dharmodgata! It is impossible for such persons, while remaining in applied and sustained thought (vitarka-vicāra), to further conceptualize, infer, or retain as objects of memory those states that lie beyond applied and sustained thought.”
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, he further spoke these verses:
"Self-realized is the signless dharma, Transcending words and cutting off the four propositions;
The non-contentious dharma is the universal characteristic, Surpassing all realms of vitarka and vicāra."
Chapter Three: Resolving the Section on Transcending Identity and Difference. At that time, the Bodhisattva Viśeṣamati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
These words are a correct exposition, profound and marvelous.
As the World-Honored One has taught, this is the true principle—subtle, profound, and difficult to penetrate—namely, that it transcends the characteristics of identity and difference.
“World-Honored One!
At one time, I saw a great assembly of Bodhisattvas in a certain region practicing the path to enlightenment while dwelling on the Stage of Aspiration and Delight (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*).

They had gathered and sat together in that place, desiring to deliberate upon whether the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena and the phenomena of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-dharma*) are identical or distinct.”
At that time, among the assembly, there were bodhisattvas who spoke these words:
"This mark of reality is not different from all conditioned phenomena.
Furthermore, other bodhisattvas said:
"The true characteristic and the practice are not one.
Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who give rise to a mind of doubt, neither believing in identity nor difference, and speak these words:
"Within this matter of identity and difference, who speaks the truth?"
Who speaks of the false?
What is right practice?
What is wrong practice?
"Should one hold that they are identical?
Or should one hold that they are different?
"World-Honored One! [he asked.]
Seeing this, I reflected: "These good sons are like infants and fools—without discernment, without understanding, and not acting in accordance with the Dharma."

Why is this? Because these sons of good family have not yet attained thorough penetration into the subtle, profound, and true Dharma, which transcends the characteristics of identity and difference with respect to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
After the Bodhisattva had spoken thus, the Buddha immediately addressed him, saying: "So it is, Viśeṣamati!
So it is that these sons of good family are like infants and fools—without discernment, without understanding, and not practicing in accordance with reality."
The Tathāgata has realized that the subtle, profound, and true Dharma is equal to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), transcending the characteristics of identity and difference.
Why is this so, Pure Wisdom?

If one holds such a view, it is impossible to rely upon the phenomena of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) to cultivate the contemplation of ultimate reality and thereby attain or realize the principle of *tathatā*. Why is this?
"Vimalamati! If suchness were not distinct from the characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-lakṣaṇa*), then all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) should perceive suchness.
Furthermore, all sentient beings, while still in the stage of ordinary beings, should attain unsurpassed *nirvāṇa* as easily as if it were already established."
Furthermore, all sentient beings in their state as ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) should also be able to attain unsurpassed enlightenment.

If the characteristic of true suchness (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*) were different from the characteristic of phenomenal activity (*saṃskāra-lakṣaṇa*), then all noble ones (*ārya*) who have already perceived true suchness would be unable to suppress and eliminate phenomenal activity;

because they could not suppress and eliminate the various characteristics of phenomenal activity, even though they perceive the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), they would be unable to liberate themselves from the fetters of manifold signs (*nimitta-bandhana*).
If one does not attain liberation from the various signs, one will also not be liberated from the fetters of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*);
if one is not liberated from these two kinds of fetters, then one cannot attain the unsurpassed, peaceful *nirvāṇa* without remainder, nor can one attain unsurpassed *bodhi*.
“Viśuddhamati! Because ordinary beings do not perceive suchness, while in the stage of an ordinary being they cannot attain unsurpassed nirvāṇa as it truly is, nor can they attain unsurpassed bodhi.”
For this reason, the principle of true suchness (*tathatā*) and all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are one; this is not correct.
If someone were to say:
"True suchness and the characteristics of conditioned phenomena are not different," [it would be so].
Because of this meaning, one should know that such a person acts contrary to the principle of correct reasoning.
"Furthermore, Pure Wisdom!

All noble ones, by virtue of seeing True Suchness (tathatā), have already been able to subdue and extinguish the phenomenal characteristics (lakṣaṇa) of all dharmas; it is not because they are unable to do so."
They have already attained liberation from all fetters of signs and the afflictions of coarse heaviness;
it is not that they have not attained liberation. Through these two liberations, they have already attained unsurpassed, tranquil nirvāṇa, up to and including the attainment of unsurpassed bodhi.
Therefore, the claim that suchness is different from its phenomenal aspects is incorrect.
If someone were to say: "Suchness is different from its phenomenal aspects," [it would be wrong].
For this reason, you should know that such a person acts contrary to the principle of correct reasoning.
Furthermore, Pure Wisdom!

If true suchness were not distinct from the characteristics of conditioned activity, then just as the characteristics of activity fall into the category of delusive characteristics, the true characteristic would likewise fall into the category of delusive characteristics.
Furthermore, Viśālamati!

If the characteristic of suchness were different from the characteristic of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), then suchness would not be the universal characteristic of all conditioned phenomena. Viśālamati!
Because this suchness does not fall into the characteristics of delusion, yet serves as the universal characteristic of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
for this reason, the propositions that suchness and conditioned phenomena are either identical or different are both untenable.
If someone were to say:
"Suchness and conditioned phenomena are both identical and different," for this reason one should know that such a person does not practice in accordance with reality.
"Furthermore, Viśuddhamati!

If suchness were not different from the characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), then just as the true nature of reality (*tattvalakṣaṇa*) pervades all conditioned phenomena without distinction, so too would the characteristics of conditioned phenomena likewise pervade them without distinction."

Therefore, practitioners cultivating contemplation should not, among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), transcend these [four]—seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing—to cultivate a superior, true contemplation.

Furthermore, if the characteristic of True Suchness (*tathatā*) were different from the characteristic of conditioned phenomena, then for that reason, all conditioned phenomena would merely be non-self and devoid of intrinsic nature, and thus would not be real.
Furthermore, at one time, the categories of the pure and the impure each have their own distinct characteristics.
O Pure Wisdom!

Because the characteristics of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are merely distinct and not pervasive, when a practitioner of meditation observes within these conditioned phenomena, they transcend what is seen, heard, sensed, and known to cultivate the supreme, true contemplation. Since it is revealed that all conditioned phenomena are without self and without intrinsic nature, this is the truth; thus, even the categories of the pure and the impure do not possess distinct characteristics at one and the same time.
For this reason, the claim that suchness and conditioned phenomena are both identical and different is incorrect.
If anyone were to say that suchness and conditioned phenomena are both identical and different, one should know that such a person does not practice in accordance with reality.
“Viśuddhamati! For example, the white color of a conch shell cannot be established as being either identical to or different from the shell itself;
it is likewise with red color and gold—neither identical nor different.”
For example, the sound of a vīṇā is exquisite and beautiful, yet it cannot be established as being either identical to or different from the vīṇā;
again, like aloeswood, its fragrance is lovely, yet it cannot be established as being either identical to or different from the aloeswood;
likewise, like the mālīca fruit, its taste is pungent and spicy, yet it cannot be established as being either identical to or different from the mālīca.
The astringency of the harītakī fruit is also like this.
Furthermore, it is like cotton wool: its touch is soft and supple, yet it cannot be established as being either identical to or different from the cotton;
the same applies to the fact that ghee and clarified butter (sarpis) are neither identical nor different.

Furthermore, just as all that is subject to outflows is suffering, all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, and all dharmas are without self—such things as suffering and so forth cannot be established as being either identical to or different from the dharma;
likewise, just as greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and so forth lack the characteristic of tranquility, they cannot be established as being either identical to or different from it.
"Viśuddhamati!
Thus, suchness and all conditioned phenomena cannot be established as being either identical or different. Viśuddhamati!"

Such is this *tathatā*, subtle and profoundly deep, difficult to penetrate; having realized it myself, I explain it for others, establishing the true teaching, revealing and manifesting it so that its meaning becomes shallow and easy to understand.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, he further spoke these verses:
"The true reality and the phenomena of practice Are neither identical nor different, nor both.
If one clings to identity, difference, or both, One’s discourse on practice is not in accordance with reason."
"By practicing śamatha and vipaśyanā, this person is able to liberate themselves from the fetters of the coarse latencies of conceptual delusion.
Chapter Four: The Single Flavor (*Ekarasa*) from the *Vibhaṅga-sūtra*. At that time, the Buddha addressed Subhūti, saying:

“Subhūti! How many sentient beings do you see, how many do you know, who exist within the realm of sentient beings with overweening pride, and by virtue of this conceited mind, claim their own attainments?”

Furthermore, how many sentient beings do you see, how many do you know, who, within the realm of sentient beings, are free from overweening pride and do not, out of a conceited mind, claim their own attainments?
Subhūti said: "World-Honored One!

I see and I know that there are few sentient beings within the realm of sentient beings who are free from overweening pride (*adhimāna*) and who do not, out of a conceited mind, claim for themselves what they have attained."

"Bhagavān! I see and I know immeasurable, incalculable, and ineffable numbers of sentient beings who, within the realm of sentient beings, possess overweening pride and, by virtue of this conceit, claim their own attainments."
“World-Honored One!
On another occasion, I was dwelling in a remote and secluded forest hermitage when a large assembly of many bhikṣus gathered; they were staying in a hermitage not far from where I was.”

On another occasion, during the latter part of the day, I saw this great assembly gathered together, each speaking of their own practice and recording their own attainments according to the various characteristics of the dharmas they had realized.

There are certain bhikṣus who, through the realization and vision of the aggregates (*skandha*), declare their attainments—some bhikṣus realize and see the characteristics of the aggregates; some realize and see the arising of the aggregates; some realize the transformation of the aggregates; some realize and see the cessation of the aggregates; and some realize the path leading to the cessation of the aggregates—just as there are six modes of realization regarding the aggregates.
There are also bhikṣus who realize and see the sense-bases (*āyatana*), declaring their own attainments, up to the cessation of the bases and the path leading to the cessation of the bases;

or bhikṣus who realize and see dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), declaring their own attainments, up to the cessation of dependent origination and the path leading to the cessation of dependent origination.
There may be a bhikṣu who realizes and perceives the food of perception;
there may be a bhikṣu who realizes and perceives the Four Noble Truths;

there may be a bhikṣu who realizes and perceives the various elements (*dhātu*), as well as the differentiation of elements and the manifold elements, up to the cessation of elements and the path leading to the cessation of elements.

There may be a bhikṣu who realizes and sees the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), as well as their characteristics, their remedies, the path that serves as their remedy, and their cultivation; he realizes and sees the arising of the foundations of mindfulness not yet arisen, and the stability, non-forgetfulness, increase, and fulfillment of those already arisen, thereby recording his own attainment.

Just as with the realization of the foundations of mindfulness, so too regarding right effort, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the noble path—namely, the characteristics of the noble path, the remedies of the noble path, the path that serves as a remedy for the noble path, and the cultivation of the noble path—he realizes the arising of the noble path not yet arisen, he realizes the persistence of the noble path already arisen, and he realizes its non-forgetfulness, increase, fulfillment, and perfection, thereby certifying his own attainment.
“World-Honored One!
Having seen this, I reflected thus:
‘Just as these elders record their own attainments according to the various characteristics of phenomena they have realized and seen, these elders possess overweening pride.’”
"Due to this conceit, they claim their own attainment, asserting that 'this matter is certainly so. Why is this?

Because they have realized and seen the Dharma as they describe it, one should know that such persons have not yet been able to discern the single flavor of True Suchness (tathatā) as pervading all places."
“World-Honored One!
As the World-Honored One has said:
‘The single flavor of reality pervades all places; it is subtle and profound, difficult to penetrate.’”
"These words are rare and beyond all opposition.
World-Honored One!

If even those bhikṣus who diligently cultivate contemplative practice within the True Teaching of the World-Honored One find it difficult to penetrate the single flavor of reality that pervades all places; "
"How much more so for the various non-Buddhists who remain outside the True Teaching; how could they possibly realize the single flavor of ultimate reality?
The Buddha said, "It is so, Subhūti!"

Thus, having realized that which is subtle and most subtle, profound and most profound, difficult to see and most difficult to see—the single-flavored reality pervading all places—I have explained it for others, established the true teaching, revealed and manifested it, and made its meaning shallow and easy to understand.
Why is this? Subhūti!
That which is the pure realm within the five aggregates is what I describe as the "real."

Subhūti! Within the twelve bases, the twelve links of dependent origination, the four nutriments, the four truths, the various elements, the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path—within these pure realms, that which I have taught is called the ultimate reality.
This realm of purity is of a single equal flavor across all aggregates (*skandha*) and sense bases (*āyatana*), devoid of any marks of differentiation.
Just as within the aggregates and so forth up to the factors of the noble path (*āryamārgāṅga*), the realm of purity is of a single equal flavor, entirely without distinction.
Subhūti! For this reason, you should know that the single flavor of suchness pervades all places. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"

If a practicing bhikṣu has already thoroughly realized the suchness of one aggregate—the selflessness of persons and phenomena—he need not exert further effort to contemplate the suchness of each of the remaining aggregates.

Regarding the twelve bases, the twelve links of dependent origination, the four nutriments, the four truths, the various elements, and the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path—if one has already thoroughly penetrated the suchness of even a single part, namely the selflessness of persons and phenomena, there is no need to labor further to contemplate the suchness inherent in the remaining factors of the noble path.

Apart from the subsequent non-conceptual wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), there is no other contemplation capable of conforming to the contemplation of *tathatā* (suchness) by viewing all remaining phenomena as having a single flavor of reality that pervades all places.

Rather, it is solely through the subsequent non-conceptual wisdom, which conforms to the preceding non-conceptual wisdom, that one contemplates all phenomena as having a single flavor of reality, maintaining this realization until its attainment.
Subhūti! For this reason, you should know that the principle of ultimate reality pervades all places and possesses only a single flavor. Furthermore, Subhūti!

Just as the various aggregates (*skandha*) possess distinct characteristics from one another, and likewise the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the four nutriments (*āhāra*), the four truths (*satya*), the various elements (*dhātu*), the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the faculties (*indriya*), the powers (*bala*), the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*) each possess distinct characteristics; if the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena and the selflessness of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharmanairātmya*) were to possess distinct characteristics from one another, then the suchness of all phenomena and the selflessness of persons and phenomena would not constitute reality, as they would necessarily arise from causes.
If it arises from causes, it is conditioned; if it is conditioned, it is not real; if it is not real, one must seek another reality beyond it.
Subhūti! Because this reality does not arise from causes, it is not conditioned; yet it is not unreal, and within it one need not laboriously seek another reality.

Why is this? Because this Dharma is eternal; whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), and the stability of phenomena (dharmaniyāmatā) all abide forever.
Subhūti! For this reason, you should know that the single flavor of reality is equal in all places. Subhūti!

For example, just as various forms differ from one another in their manifold distinctions, within all these forms, space is without characteristics; it is without distinction and without change, possessing a single uniform nature throughout all places.
In this way, these various phenomena are each distinct and different.
You should know that within all phenomena, the single flavor of true suchness is likewise equal and without distinction.
At that time, when the World-Honored One had finished speaking this sutra, he spoke again in verse:
"The Dharma’s universal characteristic is of one flavor; All Buddhas proclaim it as equal."
If one grasps at difference within this, such a person possesses overweening pride.
The path that flows against the current of birth and death is subtle, profound, and difficult to see;
because it is shrouded by desire, defilement, and ignorance, ordinary people cannot attain it.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Having now heard from the Buddha such a profound Dharma for unraveling the knots, I have attained what I never had before; I shall receive it upon my head and uphold it."
"Bhagavān, what should this sutra be named?
How should it be upheld?"
The Buddha told Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva:

“This sutra is titled ‘The Correct Teaching of Definitive Meaning’; it is also titled ‘The Correct Teaching of the Reality of True Objects and Wisdom’; and it is also titled ‘The Correct Teaching on the Basis of the Ten Stages and the Pāramitās.’”
"You all should uphold it in this manner.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, eighty thousand bodhisattvas all attained the Mahāyāna Majestic Virtue Samādhi; immeasurable and boundless multitudes of bodhisattvas attained the endurance of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); countless sentient beings attained liberation of mind from the various outflows (*āsrava*); and countless sentient beings gave rise to a heart of faith and joy toward the Mahāyāna Dharma.
The Scripture on the Elucidation of the Sections Spoken by the Buddha (Buddhabhāṣita-vibhaṅga-sūtra)
